label: <DEL> step when the first two original tokens are both from {v,e,x,h,i,j,3,m,u}
explanation: Mostly a delimiter-step unit: 85% of its activations and 89% of activation mass fall on the <DEL> step (rate 10.8% there, vs about 0.1-0.3% elsewhere). Whether it fires at <DEL> depends on the start of the sequence about to be copied. The first output token (orig(0)) has the strongest effect (v 8.8x lift, then e, x, h, i, j, 3, m, u), and the second token (next_out) has a similar ranking. Firing when both of the first two tokens are in that set gives dev P 0.72 / R 0.51 / F1 0.60 (mass recall 0.65). The top examples begin with v and then another set token (x v v.., v h v.., h v v..). It fires somewhat more at long L (8-9) and very short L (3). A smaller tail fires at the first copy step (recall_idx 1, about 8% of mass) when the remaining tokens are similar, plus scattered weak firing during the original phase (mostly on input q). It does not fire at t=0 or late in the copy phase. The two-token rule is a simplification of what looks like a graded score over the first few tokens, so precision and recall are both incomplete.

scorecard.summary: Graded preference over the token being output (most: v, h, e, x, i, j; least: q, y, l, 2) and the next token to output (most: v, h, e, j, u, i; least: y, p, a, q); timing cues that raise it most: recall_idx=1, L=9 & t=10, L=6 & t=4.
